title: Hybrid LRU + Probabilistic Prefix Coordinator for Cross-Request KV Reuse
creator: Asha Iyer
description: Design and implement a coordinated prefix cache layer (Prefix Coordinator) that combines a tiny LRU admission window with a probabilistic deduplication index (Bloom + locality hash) to maximize cross-request KV reuse while bounding GPU memory overhead and avoiding excessive CPU/GPU sync. Target workloads: high-throughput chat and multi-turn completion workloads with varying template reuse and tenant skew.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end integration into the runtime serving path with a configurable coordinator enabled flag
Measured increase in KV reuse hit-rate >= 15% on internal chat benchmark (baseline: current shared-kv without coordinator)
End-to-end 95th percentile tail token latency regression <= 5% on p100, a100-lb, and T4 profiles
GPU memory overhead from coordinator metadata < 4% at 99th percentile for production instance mixes
Automated unit and integration tests for admission, false-positive behavior, eviction coordination, and fallbacks
Operational dashboards for coordinator hit-rate, bloom false-positive rate, admission churn, and memory footprint
design_decisions: Use a tiny LRU admission window (per-shard, on-CPU) to rapidly onboard hot prefix fragments and avoid polluting the main GPU-resident slab with one-off prefixes
Maintain a probabilistic dedupe index: a compact Bloom filter sharded by model+tenant + locality hash to detect near-duplicate prefix fragments before attempting GPU residency
Store canonical prefix fragments in existing GPU slab allocator; coordinator only stores compact metadata (fingerprints, resident-slab refs, refcounts) to minimize GPU memory impact
Prioritize index/eviction work on background threads with backpressure hints to the serving thread to avoid blocking critical request paths
Deterministic fallback: on coordinator miss, serve request normally and opportunistically schedule an asynchronous prefetch if heuristics indicate high reuse probability
Expose tuning knobs (admission window size, bloom bits per entry, residency threshold, async-prefetch budget) via runtime config and Console UI
migration_plan: Phase A: Feature gated rollout as read-only: coordinator observes and emits telemetry without changing admission (2 weeks)
Phase B: Enable admission on a small percentage of requests (1%) in canary region; monitor hit-rate and tail latency for regressions (2 weeks)
Phase C: Ramp to 10% then 50% with increased monitoring; enable async prefetch after confirming low false-positive costs (2-4 weeks)
Phase D: Global rollout with default conservative config; provide per-customer opt-out for Dedicated/Private customers
Rollback plan: feature toggle to instantly disable coordinator and flush all coordinator-specific metadata; ensure fallback path is exercised in tests
rollout_plan: Initial experiments on dev and perf clusters using synthetic workload and Shadow traffic from staging services
Canary with 1 node pool serving non-critical tenants, collect dashboards and A/B metrics
Progressive rollout tied to strict SLO gates: if any gate fails (latency or OOM), auto-rollback
Post-rollout: 2-week stability watch and follow-up tuning sprint
benchmarks: Internal chat-v2 benchmark: multi-tenant, multi-turn mix (50K requests), compare baseline vs coordinator-enabled
Memory pressure tests with synthetic long-prefix workloads to validate coordinator memory cap behavior
Tail latency microbenchmarks for admission path under lock contention scenarios
False-positive sensitivity sweep by varying Bloom bits-per-key to find optimal trade-off curve
risks: Bloom false positives could cause unnecessary prefetches and GPU residency churn if bits-per-key are too low
Admission window too small may fail to capture mid-frequency prefixes, too large may evict useful fragments from slab
Coordination background tasks adding CPU overhead on host machines with tight CPU budgets
Incorrect refcounting across shards leading to premature eviction or memory leaks
Edge-case interaction with multi-tenant eviction policies causing noisy neighbor effects
